course.title: Docker Certified Associate — the Container Yard
course.description: Ship one small web app in containers as a four-person team: build an image, push it to a registry, orchestrate the stack, network and persist it, scan and harden the image, and hand it over. Built for the DCA.
course.audience: Build, orchestrate and hand over one containerized stack as a four-person team — everyone runs every command; the focus decides which record you lead.

roles.name: Images (Build Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the image record: the Dockerfile, the tags, the registry and the scan.

roles.name: Orchestration (Stack Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the stack record: Compose, the Swarm services, scaling and rollback.

roles.name: Networking & Storage (Platform Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the network and volume record: the container networks, the ports and the data.

roles.name: Operations (Records Lead)
roles.mission: Leads the records that outlive the yard: hardening, the runbook, custody and handover.

tasks.title: Install Docker Engine and Compose
tasks.objective: Install Docker Engine and the Compose plugin, and confirm both report their versions.
definitionOfDone: docker version shows a client and a server
docker compose version shows the plugin
The install method and version are recorded

steps.title: Install Docker and read its version
steps.description: Install Docker and read its version
steps.instruction: Install Docker Engine for your operating system from the official docs, then confirm the client and the daemon are both there.

commands.cmd: docker version --format "{{.Client.Version}} / {{.Server.Version}}"
commands.explain: Prints the client and server (daemon) versions; both must be present.

commands.cmd: docker compose version
commands.explain: Confirms the Compose v2 plugin is installed.

steps.expectedOutput:
27.3.1 / 27.3.1
Docker Compose version v2.29.7
steps.whatItMeans: The client talks to the daemon; a client with no server is the most common first fault. Both versions on one line prove the install.

fixes.symptom: docker says it cannot connect to the daemon?
fixes.fix: Start the Docker service (or Docker Desktop), and add your user to the docker group, then open a new terminal.

fixes.symptom: compose is not a docker command?
fixes.fix: Install the docker-compose-plugin package; Compose v2 is a plugin, not the old standalone binary.

tasks.title: Prove the engine runs a container
tasks.objective: Run the hello-world image and list it, so the engine is proven before any real work.
definitionOfDone: hello-world runs and prints its message
The image is listed locally
The run is recorded in the register

steps.title: Run hello-world and list the image
steps.description: Run hello-world and list the image
steps.instruction: Run the hello-world container, then list the images now on the machine.

commands.cmd: docker run --rm hello-world | grep -i "working"
commands.explain: Pulls and runs the test image; the line proves the whole pull-run loop works.
commands.sample: Hello from Docker! This message shows that your installation appears to be working correctly.

commands.cmd: docker images --format "{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}} {{.Size}}" | head
commands.explain: Lists local images with their sizes.

steps.expectedOutput:
Hello from Docker! This message shows that your installation appears to be working correctly.
hello-world:latest 20.4kB
steps.whatItMeans: If hello-world runs, the daemon can pull, create and run a container. Everything else is a bigger version of this.

outputHighlights.label: The pull-run loop works end to end.

tasks.title: Know your team, your focus and the folder
tasks.objective: Agree who leads which record, name the app, and make the yard folder every artifact goes in.
definitionOfDone: Each of the four focuses has a named member
The app has a name in the pattern yard-t<team>
The yard folder exists with a week-0 to week-4 layout

steps.title: Pick the focus and name the app
steps.description: Four names against four focuses, and an app name the whole team uses from now on.
steps.instruction: Agree who leads Images, Orchestration, Networking & Storage and Operations. Name the app yard-t and your team number, and write both into the register.
steps.expectedOutput: Four names against four focuses, and an app name the whole team uses from now on.
steps.whatItMeans: A focus is the record a member leads and reviews, not the only work they do. Everyone runs every command.

steps.title: Make the yard folder
steps.description: Make the yard folder
steps.instruction: Create the yard folder with a subfolder for each week. Every Dockerfile, compose file and output goes under the week it belongs to.

commands.cmd: mkdir -p yard-t1/week-{0,1,2,3,4} && ls yard-t1
commands.explain: Five week folders in one command, then reads them back. Replace t1 with your team number.

steps.expectedOutput: week-0  week-1  week-2  week-3  week-4
steps.whatItMeans: An artifact nobody can find is an artifact nobody can hash. The folder is the first custody control.

tasks.title: Build and tag the app image
tasks.objective: Write a Dockerfile for the app, build it, and tag it with a semantic version, not just latest.
definitionOfDone: The image builds from a Dockerfile with no error
It carries a semantic tag as well as latest
The image size and layer count are recorded

steps.title: Build the image from a Dockerfile
steps.description: Build the image from a Dockerfile
steps.instruction: Write a Dockerfile for the app, then build it and tag it with a version.

commands.cmd: docker build -t yard-t1/app:1.0.0 -t yard-t1/app:latest . && docker images yard-t1/app
commands.explain: Builds the image, applies two tags, and lists them.
commands.sample:
REPOSITORY    TAG      IMAGE ID       CREATED         SIZE
yard-t1/app   1.0.0    a1b2c3d4e5f6   2 seconds ago   84MB
yard-t1/app   latest   a1b2c3d4e5f6   2 seconds ago   84MB

steps.expectedOutput:
REPOSITORY    TAG      IMAGE ID       CREATED         SIZE
yard-t1/app   1.0.0    a1b2c3d4e5f6   2 seconds ago   84MB
yard-t1/app   latest   a1b2c3d4e5f6   2 seconds ago   84MB
steps.whatItMeans: A semantic tag is what lets you roll back to a known build; latest alone is a build you can never name again.

outputHighlights.label: The build is tagged with a version you can roll back to.

fixes.symptom: The build fails on a COPY line?
fixes.fix: The path is relative to the build context (the final dot). Check the file exists in the directory you built from.

fixes.symptom: Every build is slow?
fixes.fix: Order the Dockerfile so the least-changing layers come first; put COPY of source after dependency install so the cache holds.

steps.title: Shrink it with a multi-stage build
steps.description: Shrink it with a multi-stage build
steps.instruction: Add a build stage and a slim runtime stage, rebuild, and compare the size.

commands.cmd: docker build -t yard-t1/app:1.0.0 . && docker image inspect yard-t1/app:1.0.0 --format "{{.Size}} bytes, {{len .RootFS.Layers}} layers"
commands.explain: Rebuilds with the multi-stage Dockerfile and prints the size and layer count.

steps.expectedOutput: 84000000 bytes, 7 layers
steps.whatItMeans: A multi-stage build leaves the compiler and the source behind, so the image that ships is smaller and has less to attack.

handoff.note: Your section of the Image Build & Registry Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Push it to a registry
tasks.objective: Run a local registry, push the tagged image to it, and pull it back to prove the round trip.
prerequisites: The tagged app image from the build task
definitionOfDone: A registry is running and the image is pushed to it
The image pulls back by tag
The pushed digest is recorded

steps.title: Run a registry and push the image
steps.description: Run a registry and push the image
steps.instruction: Start a local registry container, retag the image for it, and push.

commands.cmd: docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --name registry registry:2 && docker tag yard-t1/app:1.0.0 localhost:5000/app:1.0.0 && docker push localhost:5000/app:1.0.0
commands.explain: Starts a registry, retags the image for it, and pushes; the digest prints at the end.

steps.expectedOutput: 1.0.0: digest: sha256:9f8e7d6c... size: 1365
steps.whatItMeans: A registry is how an image gets from the build machine to everywhere it runs; the digest is the one name that never changes.

outputHighlights.label: The immutable name of what you pushed.

fixes.symptom: push says connection refused?
fixes.fix: The registry container is not up; check `docker ps` and that port 5000 is published.

steps.title: Pull it back by tag
steps.description: Pull it back by tag
steps.instruction: Remove the local image and pull it back from the registry to prove the round trip.

commands.cmd: docker rmi localhost:5000/app:1.0.0 && docker pull localhost:5000/app:1.0.0 | tail -1
commands.explain: Deletes the local copy, then pulls it back from the registry.
commands.sample: Status: Downloaded newer image for localhost:5000/app:1.0.0

steps.expectedOutput: Status: Downloaded newer image for localhost:5000/app:1.0.0
steps.whatItMeans: An image you cannot pull back is an image you have not really shipped. The round trip is the proof.

handoff.note: Your section of the Image Build & Registry Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Configure the daemon and logging
tasks.objective: Read the daemon configuration — storage driver, logging driver, log limits — and record it.
definitionOfDone: The storage and logging drivers are read from the daemon
A log size limit is set so a container cannot fill the disk
Both are recorded

steps.title: Read the daemon configuration
steps.description: Read the daemon configuration
steps.instruction: Read the storage driver, the logging driver and the root directory from the daemon.

commands.cmd: docker info --format "storage={{.Driver}} logging={{.LoggingDriver}} root={{.DockerRootDir}}"
commands.explain: Prints the storage driver, logging driver and data root in one line.

steps.expectedOutput: storage=overlay2 logging=json-file root=/var/lib/docker
steps.whatItMeans: The storage driver decides how layers are stored; the logging driver decides where container output goes. A team that knows both is not surprised by a full disk.

steps.title: Cap the log size so a container cannot fill the disk
steps.description: Cap the log size so a container cannot fill the disk
steps.instruction: Run a container with a log size limit and confirm the limit is applied.

commands.cmd: docker run -d --name capped --log-opt max-size=10m --log-opt max-file=3 yard-t1/app:1.0.0 && docker inspect capped --format "{{.HostConfig.LogConfig.Config}}"
commands.explain: Runs with a rotated, size-capped log and reads the setting back.

steps.expectedOutput: map[max-file:3 max-size:10m]
steps.whatItMeans: An uncapped container log is the classic way a box runs out of disk at 3 a.m. Ten megabytes, three files, is a safe default.

handoff.note: Your section of the Image Build & Registry Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Compose the multi-container stack
tasks.objective: Write a Compose file for the app and a database, bring the stack up, and confirm both services are healthy.
definitionOfDone: The Compose file defines the app and a database service
The stack comes up and both services are running
A healthcheck reports the app healthy

steps.title: Bring the stack up with Compose
steps.description: Bring the stack up with Compose
steps.instruction: Write a compose.yaml with the app and a database, then bring it up and list the services.

commands.cmd: docker compose up -d && docker compose ps --format "{{.Service}} {{.State}} {{.Health}}"
commands.explain: Starts the stack in the background and lists each service with its state and health.
commands.sample:
app running healthy
db running healthy

steps.expectedOutput:
app running healthy
db running healthy
steps.whatItMeans: Compose turns a page of docker run flags into one file the whole team edits and version-controls. The stack is now one command.

outputHighlights.label: The healthcheck says the app is actually serving, not just started.

fixes.symptom: The app starts before the database is ready?
fixes.fix: A depends_on with condition: service_healthy, plus a db healthcheck, makes the app wait for a ready database, not just a started one.

handoff.note: Your section of the Stack & Orchestration Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Deploy it to a Swarm
tasks.objective: Initialise a single-node Swarm, deploy the stack as services, and see the replicas scheduled.
prerequisites: The Compose stack that comes up cleanly
definitionOfDone: A Swarm is initialised and the node is a manager
The stack is deployed as Swarm services
The replicas show as running

steps.title: Init the Swarm and deploy the stack
steps.description: Init the Swarm and deploy the stack
steps.instruction: Initialise the Swarm, deploy the stack to it, and list the services with their replica counts.

commands.cmd: docker swarm init 2>/dev/null; docker stack deploy -c compose.yaml yard && docker stack services yard --format "{{.Name}} {{.Replicas}}"
commands.explain: Starts Swarm, deploys the stack as services, and shows replica counts.

steps.expectedOutput:
yard_app 2/2
yard_db 1/1
steps.whatItMeans: Swarm is Docker’s own orchestrator: a service is a desired number of identical tasks, and Swarm keeps that many running.

outputHighlights.label: Both requested replicas of the app are running.

fixes.symptom: Replicas stay 0/2?
fixes.fix: Run `docker service ps yard_app --no-trunc` to read why a task will not schedule — usually an image the node cannot pull.

handoff.note: Your section of the Stack & Orchestration Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Scale it, and roll a bad update back
tasks.objective: Scale the app service up, roll out a bad image, watch it fail, and roll back to the working tag.
prerequisites: The stack deployed as Swarm services
definitionOfDone: The app service scales to more replicas
A bad update is rolled out and then rolled back
The rollback returns the service to the working tag

steps.title: Scale the app up
steps.description: Scale the app up
steps.instruction: Scale the app service to four replicas and confirm the count.

commands.cmd: docker service scale yard_app=4 && docker service ls --filter name=yard_app --format "{{.Name}} {{.Replicas}}"
commands.explain: Scales the service and reads the new replica count back.

steps.expectedOutput: yard_app 4/4
steps.whatItMeans: Scaling is one command because a service is just a number of identical tasks; Swarm schedules the extra three.

steps.title: Roll a bad update back
steps.description: Roll a bad update back
steps.instruction: Update the service to a broken tag, see it fail to converge, then roll back to the working tag.

commands.cmd: docker service update --image localhost:5000/app:broken yard_app; docker service rollback yard_app && docker service ls --filter name=yard_app --format "{{.Image}}"
commands.explain: Deploys a bad image, then rolls back; the image shown is the working tag again.

steps.expectedOutput: localhost:5000/app:1.0.0
steps.whatItMeans: Rollback is the whole point of a rolling update: a bad deploy is one command away from the last good one, with no scramble.

handoff.note: Your section of the Stack & Orchestration Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Wire the network and resolve by name
tasks.objective: Put the containers on a user-defined network and prove one resolves the other by service name.
definitionOfDone: The services share a user-defined network
One container resolves the other by name
The network is recorded with its subnet

steps.title: Resolve a service by name
steps.description: Resolve a service by name
steps.instruction: From the app container, resolve the database by its service name to prove embedded DNS works.

commands.cmd: docker compose exec app getent hosts db || docker compose exec app ping -c1 db
commands.explain: Looks up the db service name from inside the app container; a user network gives it an address.

commands.cmd: docker network inspect yard_default --format "{{range .IPAM.Config}}{{.Subnet}}{{end}}"
commands.explain: Prints the subnet the stack network uses.

steps.whatItMeans: On a user-defined network, containers reach each other by service name through Docker’s embedded DNS. On the default bridge they cannot.

outputHighlights.label: The name resolves to a container address.

fixes.symptom: The name does not resolve?
fixes.fix: The containers are on the default bridge, which has no name resolution. Put them on a shared user-defined network (Compose does this by default).

handoff.note: Your section of the Networking & Storage Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Persist the data in a volume
tasks.objective: Put the database on a named volume and prove the data survives the container being recreated.
definitionOfDone: The database writes to a named volume
The data survives a container recreate
The volume is recorded by name

steps.title: Prove the data survives a recreate
steps.description: Prove the data survives a recreate
steps.instruction: Write a row to the database, recreate the container, and confirm the row is still there because it lives on a volume.

commands.cmd: docker volume ls --filter name=yard --format "{{.Name}}" && docker compose up -d --force-recreate db && echo "recreated — data on the volume persists"
commands.explain: Lists the named volume, recreates the db container, and the volume keeps the data.
commands.sample:
yard_dbdata
recreated — data on the volume persists

steps.expectedOutput:
yard_dbdata
recreated — data on the volume persists
steps.whatItMeans: A container is disposable; its writable layer dies with it. Anything that must survive goes on a named volume, not in the container.

fixes.symptom: The data was gone after recreate?
fixes.fix: The database path is not mounted to the named volume. Check the volumes: mapping in the compose file points at the real data directory.

handoff.note: Your section of the Networking & Storage Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Work a connectivity fault, one change per row
tasks.objective: A published port does not answer. Work it the method way: one theory, one change, one result per row, failures kept.
prerequisites: A stack where a published port does not answer
definitionOfDone: The symptom is written exactly, before any theory
Every attempt is a row: theory, the one change, the result
At least one theory was wrong and the row says so
The fix is proved with a successful request to the port

steps.title: Write the symptom exactly
steps.description: The log opens with the exact failing request and error, and no theory yet.
steps.instruction: Before any theory, write exactly what fails: the request, the port, and the error returned.
steps.expectedOutput: The log opens with the exact failing request and error, and no theory yet.
steps.whatItMeans: The method starts with the symptom written down, because the first theory is wrong half the time and nobody remembers the exact error after three changes.

steps.title: Change one thing per row and record the result
steps.description: Change one thing per row and record the result
steps.instruction: Write one theory, change exactly one thing to test it, and record the result. A wrong theory gets the next row.

commands.cmd: docker port yard_app; docker compose logs --tail 20 app; curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8080/
commands.explain: Reads the published port mapping, the recent app logs, and the HTTP status; compares against the theory.

steps.whatItMeans: One change per row is what makes the log trustworthy: you can always say which change fixed it. The same method A+ uses on hardware.

outputHighlights.label: The port answers once the mapping matches the port the app listens on.

fixes.symptom: The port maps but still no answer?
fixes.fix: The published container port must match the port the app listens on inside. The logs line shows the real listen port.

handoff.note: Your section of the Container Troubleshooting Log, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Scan the image and read the findings
tasks.objective: Scan the image for known vulnerabilities, read the high findings, and decide what to do about each.
definitionOfDone: The image is scanned and the finding counts are recorded
Each high finding has a decision: patch, accept or replace the base
The scan output is saved

steps.title: Scan the image
steps.description: Scan the image
steps.instruction: Scan the app image and read the count of findings by severity.

commands.cmd: docker scout cves yard-t1/app:1.0.0 2>/dev/null | grep -iE "critical|high" | tee week-4/scan.txt || echo "use: docker scout quickview yard-t1/app:1.0.0"
commands.explain: Scans the image and prints the critical and high findings, saving them.

steps.whatItMeans: An image inherits every vulnerability in its base and packages. Scanning is how you find them before an attacker does.

outputHighlights.label: A high-severity finding to own or fix.

fixes.symptom: docker scout is not available?
fixes.fix: Any scanner works (Trivy, Grype). Record the tool and the counts; the decision matters more than the brand.

handoff.note: Your section of the Image Security & Hardening Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Run it least-privileged, secrets out
tasks.objective: Run the app as a non-root user, drop capabilities, and keep the secret out of the image.
definitionOfDone: The container runs as a non-root user
No secret is baked into the image
The base-image decision is recorded

steps.title: Prove it runs as a non-root user
steps.description: Prove it runs as a non-root user
steps.instruction: Run the container and read the user it runs as; it must not be root.

commands.cmd: docker run --rm --user 10001 --read-only --cap-drop ALL yard-t1/app:1.0.0 id -u
commands.explain: Runs the container as a non-root uid with a read-only root and no capabilities; prints the uid.

steps.whatItMeans: A container that runs as root runs as root on the host if it escapes. A non-root user, dropped capabilities and a read-only root shrink the blast radius.

fixes.symptom: The app crashes as non-root?
fixes.fix: It is writing to a path it no longer owns. Give that path a writable volume or a tmpfs, not root.

steps.title: Prove no secret is baked into the image
steps.description: Prove no secret is baked into the image
steps.instruction: Search the image history and environment for a secret, and confirm the secret is supplied at run time instead.

commands.cmd: docker history --no-trunc yard-t1/app:1.0.0 | grep -i -E "password|secret|token" && echo "FOUND — fix it" || echo "no secret in the image layers"
commands.explain: Scans the build history for a baked-in secret; the clean result is the one you want.
commands.sample: no secret in the image layers

steps.expectedOutput: no secret in the image layers
steps.whatItMeans: A secret in a build layer is in the image forever, even if a later layer deletes it. Secrets come in at run time, never at build time.

handoff.note: Your section of the Image Security & Hardening Record, for the review that approves it.

tasks.title: Hand the stack over
tasks.objective: Assemble the handover record: what the stack is, how to run, scale and recover it, and a hashed custody row for every artifact.
prerequisites: Every other record of the course, filled
definitionOfDone: The record says what the stack is, how to run, scale and recover it
Every artifact has a custody row with its hash
The stack is torn down cleanly at the end

steps.title: Write what the stack is and how to run it
steps.description: A one-page record a new team could run the stack from, including how to recover it.
steps.instruction: Write the stack in one page: the image and tag, the services, the networks and volumes, how to bring it up, scale it and recover it.
steps.expectedOutput: A one-page record a new team could run the stack from, including how to recover it.
steps.whatItMeans: The handover is the document the next team reads before touching the stack. Written honestly, it saves them the month you just spent.

steps.title: Hash every artifact for custody
steps.description: Hash every artifact for custody
steps.instruction: Hash every file in the yard folder so the handover carries a custody row that proves what was delivered.

commands.cmd: find yard-t1 -type f -exec sha256sum {} + | tee week-4/custody.txt | wc -l && ls week-4/custody.txt
commands.explain: Hashes every artifact and counts them, writing the custody list for the record.

steps.expectedOutput:
14
week-4/custody.txt
steps.whatItMeans: A hash is what lets anyone, months later, prove the file in hand is the file delivered. It is the last control of the course.

outputHighlights.label: Every artifact hashed into one custody list.

steps.title: Tear the stack down cleanly
steps.description: Tear the stack down cleanly
steps.instruction: Remove the stack, the volumes and the registry so nothing is left running, and confirm it is gone.

commands.cmd: docker stack rm yard; docker compose down -v; docker rm -f registry 2>/dev/null; docker ps --format "{{.Names}}" | grep -E "yard|registry" || echo "all torn down"
commands.explain: Removes the stack, the compose resources and volumes, and the registry, then confirms nothing is left.

steps.expectedOutput: all torn down
steps.whatItMeans: Leaving a stack and its volumes running after handover is how a laptop fills up and a stale service answers a real request. Clean teardown is accountability.

fixes.symptom: You want to keep the data for the portfolio demo?
fixes.fix: Export the volume to a tarball first with `docker run --rm -v yard_dbdata:/d -v $PWD:/out busybox tar czf /out/dbdata.tgz /d`, then tear down.

steps.title: Write the Portfolio
steps.description: The repository, the case study, three resume bullets, the diagram and the skills shown, on the shared Portfolio form.
steps.instruction: Fill the Portfolio with the whole team.
instructionList: Paste the link to the team repository, e.g. https://github.com/org/capstone-team01, that holds the configuration and documents.
Write the case study in two hundred words or more: the problem, what was built, the decisions, the result.
Write three resume bullets, each an action, a tool and a measurable result, e.g. "closed 14 of 15 findings".
Name the diagram the case study refers to, then list the skills demonstrated with the evidence for each.
steps.expectedOutput: The Portfolio is filled: a repository link, a case study of two hundred words or more, three bullets, the diagram named, three or more skills with evidence.

docs.title: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010: architecture description
docs.lookFor: What an architecture description must identify: stakeholders, concerns, viewpoints and the rationale for decisions.

DOMAINS.evidence: A verification record per step: the output hash, the tokens matched, the attempts, and a receipt in cloud mode.

DOMAINS.label: Professional execution
DOMAINS.definition: Procedures followed to standard, steps in order, first pastes, evidence named, checks met, documents controlled, work on time.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member follow the runbook as written and deliver on the calendar?
DOMAINS.evidence: The order of verification stamps, the attempts, the file names, the Definition-of-Done checks, the control block and the cohort due dates.

DOMAINS.label: Problem solving
DOMAINS.definition: Faults logged and resolved, steps verified after a failed paste, stuck flags cleared, and the minutes from first paste to proof.
DOMAINS.asks: When something breaks, does this member find and fix it, and how long does it take?
DOMAINS.evidence: Fault, incident and triage rows with their outcome column, retries that verified, the append-only flag history and two stamps per step.

DOMAINS.label: Thought process
DOMAINS.definition: Decisions recorded against at least three options with rationale, rejected options, risk and rollback, and reasons written on change rows.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member weigh options, say why, and plan the way back?
DOMAINS.evidence: Decision blocks with the option chosen, who chose it and when, the answers to the supporting questions, and the form lifecycle.

DOMAINS.label: Architecture and design
DOMAINS.definition: Design briefs, topologies, IP plans, bills of materials, decision records and as-built documents drafted, approved and issued.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member design a system and write it down so another team can build it?
DOMAINS.evidence: The architecture and configuration forms of the role: rows filled, checks met, approved or issued, with the decisions on them.

DOMAINS.label: Team and communication
DOMAINS.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected, peer reviews given, steps ticked for teammates, reports filed, notes written, handovers issued.
DOMAINS.asks: Does this member hand work on cleanly, review others and hold their lane?
DOMAINS.evidence: The lifecycle rows with who moved what, the hand-offs and their forms, the peer review queue, the reports and the notes.

DOMAINS.label: Learning and retention
DOMAINS.definition: Skills proved on a second task, verified again a week or more later, reused in another course, and the pace month on month.
DOMAINS.asks: Is this member still learning, and keeping what was learned?
DOMAINS.evidence: The verification stamps of every skill: first and last, the tasks and courses between them, and the last two months of them.

DOMAINS.label: Professional readiness
DOMAINS.definition: The tier per record item at ten verified uses, the exam weight verified, the work-role coverage and the readiness score.
DOMAINS.asks: Can this member consistently perform at a professional level in a real work environment?
DOMAINS.evidence: Every category of the record with its verified uses across courses, the published exam weights and the work roles’ required competencies.

KPIS.label: Skills verified
KPIS.numerator: Skills with at least one step verified from pasted output.
KPIS.denominator: Skills the role practises that carry a verifiable step.
KPIS.whyMember: Each verified skill names a task where the pasted output held every expected token.
KPIS.whyCompany: Skills backed by matched output rather than a tick, with the task behind each one named.

KPIS.label: Exam weight verified
KPIS.numerator: The published exam weight of every domain with a verified step, summed.
KPIS.denominator: The published exam weight of every domain the role practises, summed.
KPIS.whyMember: Shows which share of the exam blueprint the verified work already touches.
KPIS.whyCompany: Reads the verified work against the published exam domains and their weights.

KPIS.label: Commands verified
KPIS.numerator: Verified required steps that run a command.
KPIS.denominator: Verifiable required steps that run a command.
KPIS.whyMember: Command steps proven by their output; the table below splits them by tool.
KPIS.whyCompany: Tool use proven by output, per command step, split by tool in the table.

KPIS.label: Procedures to standard
KPIS.numerator: Followed procedures whose form cites a control code and was approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Procedures followed: every check due met and document control complete.
KPIS.whyMember: A runbook followed to a named control and approved by the team; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Procedures run to a cited NIST, ISO or SOC 2 control and approved by the team.

KPIS.label: Faults resolved
KPIS.numerator: Fault, incident and triage rows whose outcome column reads resolved.
KPIS.denominator: Fault, incident and triage rows the team filled on the forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Every fault the team logged, and how many ended resolved; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Troubleshooting success read from the fault and incident records the team kept.

KPIS.label: Verified after retry
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps that took more than one paste.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps.
KPIS.whyMember: A step that failed once and was then proven: the fault was found and fixed.
KPIS.whyCompany: How often a failed first paste was followed by a verified fix.

KPIS.label: Stuck flags cleared
KPIS.numerator: Stuck flags the member raised and later cleared.
KPIS.denominator: Stuck flags the member raised.
KPIS.whyMember: Asking for help and then getting past it both count; a flag never cleared says so.
KPIS.whyCompany: Blockers raised and worked through, from the append-only flag history.

KPIS.label: Time to resolution
KPIS.numerator: The median minutes from the first paste to the verification, per verified step with both stamps.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps with both stamps; the share within the hour is the percentage.
KPIS.whyMember: The median, so one long gap moves nothing; a step left over a day is counted apart.
KPIS.whyCompany: Minutes from first attempt to proof, read from two recorded stamps, never a clock.

KPIS.label: Steps verified in order
KPIS.numerator: Tasks whose verifiable steps were verified in the authored order.
KPIS.denominator: Tasks with two or more verification records, so an order exists.
KPIS.whyMember: The procedure was run as written, step after step.
KPIS.whyCompany: Runbooks followed in order, read from the sequence of verification records.

KPIS.label: First-try verifications
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps whose first paste held every expected token.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps.
KPIS.whyMember: Shown beside retries: a step verified after several pastes counts for as much.
KPIS.whyCompany: How often the first paste matched, printed beside how often it took more than one.

KPIS.label: Files named to convention
KPIS.numerator: Hashed files named to the evidence convention.
KPIS.denominator: Hashed files.
KPIS.whyMember: Evidence an auditor can find: date, team, tool and subject in every file name.
KPIS.whyCompany: Chain-of-custody hygiene: hashed files that follow the naming convention.

KPIS.label: Definition-of-Done met
KPIS.numerator: Definition-of-Done checks met on the forms of the role.
KPIS.denominator: Checks due on those forms through the current week.
KPIS.whyMember: Every check a form must pass this week, met or not, counted for the team.
KPIS.whyCompany: Work products measured against their own acceptance checks, week by week.

KPIS.label: Decisions recorded
KPIS.numerator: Decision blocks with an option chosen by this member.
KPIS.denominator: Decision blocks on the forms of the role, each with at least three options.
KPIS.whyMember: Each decision names the options weighed, the one chosen, who chose and when.
KPIS.whyCompany: Component, configuration and architecture choices made against named alternatives.

KPIS.label: Decisions justified
KPIS.numerator: Recorded decisions with every required supporting question answered.
KPIS.denominator: Decisions recorded by this member.
KPIS.whyMember: A choice with its reason, the rejected options and the risk accepted.
KPIS.whyCompany: Judgment shown in writing: rationale, rejected options, risk and rollback per decision.

KPIS.label: Decisions approved
KPIS.numerator: Recorded decisions on a form the team approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Decisions recorded by this member.
KPIS.whyMember: The team stood behind the choice; a team fact.
KPIS.whyCompany: Decisions that passed the team’s review and were issued.

KPIS.label: Changes with rollback
KPIS.numerator: Change-record rows with a rollback or back-out written.
KPIS.denominator: Change-record rows on the forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Every change the team logged, and how many had a way back written down first.
KPIS.whyCompany: Change discipline: a rollback plan on every recorded change.

KPIS.label: Hand-offs completed
KPIS.numerator: Hand-offs whose named deliverable reached approved or issued.
KPIS.denominator: Hand-offs of the tasks of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Work handed to another role that the team then approved or issued.
KPIS.whyCompany: Cross-role hand-offs closed by an approved document.

KPIS.label: RACI respected
KPIS.numerator: Lifecycle moves the member made in the role the RACI names for that move.
KPIS.denominator: Lifecycle moves the member made on forms with a RACI.
KPIS.whyMember: Submitting as the drafter, approving as the approver: the lane was held.
KPIS.whyCompany: Role discipline on documents, read from who moved what.

KPIS.label: Peer reviews given
KPIS.numerator: Blind peer reviews the member completed.
KPIS.denominator: Peer reviews assigned to the member.
KPIS.whyMember: Reviews of other teams’ frozen work, answered question by question.
KPIS.whyCompany: Review work done for others, from the blind review queue.

KPIS.label: Teammate steps ticked
KPIS.numerator: Required steps the member ticked on another role’s tasks.
KPIS.denominator: No denominator: a count.
KPIS.whyMember: Steps done on a teammate’s task, so a lane short of hands still finished.
KPIS.whyCompany: Help given across roles, counted in steps.

KPIS.label: On time
KPIS.numerator: Tasks whose last verification fell on or before the week due date.
KPIS.denominator: Tasks with a verification; needs the cohort start date.
KPIS.whyMember: The due date comes from the cohort calendar; without one the row says so.
KPIS.whyCompany: Reliability against a calendar, read from the verification stamps and the cohort start.

KPIS.label: Document control complete
KPIS.numerator: Forms with data whose document-control block is complete.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role with data.
KPIS.whyMember: Id, version, owner, date and status on every document the team filled.
KPIS.whyCompany: Document control kept on every filled form: id, version, owner, date, status.

KPIS.label: Controls cited
KPIS.numerator: Distinct control codes on approved or issued forms the role drafts.
KPIS.denominator: Distinct control codes the forms of the role cite.
KPIS.whyMember: The published controls the approved documents cite, by code.
KPIS.whyCompany: Control codes practised through approved documents, by standard.

KPIS.label: Instructor approved
KPIS.numerator: Forms of the role whose latest instructor review is approved.
KPIS.denominator: Forms of the role.
KPIS.whyMember: Forms an instructor reviewed and approved; the latest review per form counts.
KPIS.whyCompany: Forms with an instructor verdict of approved, the latest review per form.

KPIS.label: Skills proved twice
KPIS.numerator: Skills with verified steps on two or more distinct tasks.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: A skill verified on two different tasks was carried from one context to another.
KPIS.whyCompany: Verification repeated on a second task is harder to reach by luck or by copying.

KPIS.label: Skills retained
KPIS.numerator: Skills verified again seven or more days after their first verification.
KPIS.denominator: Skills with at least one verified step.
KPIS.whyMember: Proof a week or more apart: the skill stayed.
KPIS.whyCompany: Retention read from the gap between two verification stamps on the same skill.

KPIS.label: Learning velocity
KPIS.numerator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before the page clock.
KPIS.denominator: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before those; the percentage caps at one hundred.
KPIS.whyMember: This month against last: rising, level or slowing, from the verification stamps.
KPIS.whyCompany: Pace of verified work, month on month, from recorded stamps.

KPIS.label: Profile coverage
KPIS.numerator: Required competencies of the selected work role or environment profile at verified or better.
KPIS.denominator: Required competencies the selected work role or environment profile names.
KPIS.whyMember: Measures the verified skills against a job role or a published company profile, with the untaught gap named.
KPIS.whyCompany: Coverage of the competencies a work role or an environment profile requires, read from verified steps.

KPIS.label: Values recalled
KPIS.numerator: Recall activities answered correctly: the value the team recorded, picked among distractors.
KPIS.denominator: Recall activities answered, from the checkpoints reached.
KPIS.whyMember: Weeks after recording an address, a prefix, a port or a decision, the member still knows it.
KPIS.whyCompany: Retention of the project the member built, read from answers given without the form open.

KPIS.label: Scenarios applied
KPIS.numerator: Applied scenarios answered correctly: an address inside the prefix, a free port on the host, the committed size.
KPIS.denominator: Applied scenarios offered at the checkpoints reached.
KPIS.whyMember: Takes a value the team recorded and uses it under a change the course did not script.
KPIS.whyCompany: Applied use of recorded facts, not recall alone; offered scenarios count whether or not answered.

KPIS.label: Conflicts resolved
KPIS.numerator: Conflicts the record found that the team resolved: the address, the port, the prefix, the size no longer at odds.
KPIS.denominator: Conflicts the record found at the checkpoints reached, resolved or still open.
KPIS.whyMember: A duplicate address or an over-committed host found by the platform and fixed by the team.
KPIS.whyCompany: Contradictions in the record closed, read from the record itself rather than from a claim.

KPIS.label: Minutes on task
KPIS.numerator: Whole minutes the member had tasks of this course open on a visible tab, pauses excluded.
KPIS.denominator: A count; nothing is read into it.
KPIS.whyMember: How long the work took the member, by the timer they can pause; measured, never rewarded.
KPIS.whyCompany: Time on task as context for the other rows; no score reads it.

KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Can this member operate the tools and run the procedures the job needs?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Professional execution
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: How the work was done: steps in order, first pastes, evidence named to convention, every check due met.

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Decision making
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Decisions recorded against at least three options, justified, approved by the team, and changes with a rollback written.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member weigh options, say why, and plan the way back?

KPI_FAMILIES.label: Teamwork
KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected, peer reviews given and steps ticked on teammates’ tasks.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Does this member hand work on cleanly and hold their lane in a team?

KPI_FAMILIES.definition: On time against the cohort calendar, documents controlled, controls cited, instructor approval earned.

KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Skills proved twice, retained across weeks, verified faster week on week, and the gap to a work role closing.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Is this member still learning, and keeping what was learned?

KPI_FAMILIES.definition: Values the team recorded, recalled and applied weeks later; conflicts the record found, resolved; minutes on task, measured.
KPI_FAMILIES.asks: Did this member retain what the team built, and can they apply it when something changes?

METRICS.note: A team fact; loads on the course page.

METRICS.label: Stuck flags cleared
METRICS.definition: Stuck flags the member raised and later cleared, over flags raised.
METRICS.note: R132: the flag history is append-only. R136: loads on every surface.

METRICS.label: Decisions offered
METRICS.definition: Decision blocks on the forms of the role, each with at least three options.

METRICS.label: Decisions recorded
METRICS.definition: Decision blocks with an option chosen by this member, over decision blocks on the forms of the role.
METRICS.note: The choice carries who made it and when. Loads on the course page.

METRICS.label: Decisions justified
METRICS.definition: Recorded decisions with every required supporting question answered, over decisions recorded.
METRICS.note: Loads on the course page.

METRICS.label: Decisions approved
METRICS.definition: Recorded decisions on a form the team approved or issued, over decisions recorded.
METRICS.note: Loads on the course page.

METRICS.label: Reasons written
METRICS.definition: Free-text rationale fields filled on the forms of the role, over such fields.
METRICS.note: Team rows carry no author. Loads on the course page.

METRICS.label: Review marks met
METRICS.definition: Instructor marks per rubric category that passed, over marks given on the forms of the role.
METRICS.note: R132: one mark per category per verdict, kept as history. Loads on the course page.

METRICS.label: Execution rows
METRICS.definition: In order, first try, evidence named, checks met, control complete and on time, as rows of the Professional Execution domain.

METRICS.label: Skills reused across courses
METRICS.definition: Skills verified in two or more courses, over skills verified anywhere.
METRICS.note: A portfolio fact: read across the member’s courses.

METRICS.label: Professional tier
METRICS.definition: Record items with ten or more verified uses across every course and retake, over items with any verified use.
METRICS.note: R132: the threshold is ten; below it the item reads as building, with the count.

METRICS.label: Cohort domain coverage
METRICS.definition: Per cohort, members with at least one verified step per domain, over members. Instructor aggregate.

METRICS.label: Funnel stages
METRICS.definition: Members who reached each stage in turn, from enrolled to capstone filed, over members enrolled. Instructor aggregate.
METRICS.note: Counts per cohort; nobody named.

METRICS.label: Active weeks bands
METRICS.definition: Members per band of graded weeks with any tick: none, one, two or three, four or more. Instructor aggregate.

METRICS.label: Step friction
METRICS.definition: Per verifiable step, members ticked without verification, stuck, or stopped before it, over members with the task.
METRICS.note: Steps are ordered, never people.

METRICS.label: Course verifiability
METRICS.definition: Verifiable required steps over required steps per course. Content only.

METRICS.label: Course skill coverage
METRICS.definition: Skills, tools, procedures, standards, tactics and practices per course. Content only.

METRICS.label: Cross-platform signal
METRICS.definition: A competency-level statement shared with another platform.

METRICS.label: Profile coverage
METRICS.definition: Required competencies of a work role or an environment profile at verified or better, over required; the untaught remainder is named.

METRICS.label: Skills proved twice
METRICS.definition: Skills with verified steps on two or more distinct tasks, over skills with a verified step.

METRICS.label: Skills current
METRICS.definition: Skills whose last verification falls inside the currency window, over skills verified.
METRICS.note: A window of days the page supplies; never a duration shown.

METRICS.label: Capstone filed
METRICS.definition: The course capstone document issued by the team, one per course, with the weeks cleared beside it.
METRICS.note: A team fact; loads on the course page.

METRICS.label: Ability estimate
METRICS.definition: A latent ability per objective estimated from item responses on a practice platform.
METRICS.note: The practice platform’s side; only a competency-level conclusion may cross, with consent.

METRICS.label: Readiness band
METRICS.definition: A pass-likelihood band per exam, validated against reported outcomes.
METRICS.note: The practice platform’s side; needs reported outcomes and consent.

METRICS.label: Transfer to unseen scenarios
METRICS.definition: Verified work on a scenario never practised before, over such scenarios.
METRICS.note: Needs scenario provenance per event.

METRICS.label: Unassisted verifications
METRICS.definition: Steps verified with no hint, tutor or agent assistance, over verified steps.
METRICS.note: Needs the assist level recorded per event.

METRICS.label: Rubric verdicts as events
METRICS.definition: The four category verdicts of each frozen submission, appended as events.
METRICS.note: The verdicts exist as rows today.

METRICS.label: Placement reported
METRICS.definition: Members who reported a role after a course, over members who answered with the outcome grant on.
METRICS.note: Counts only, shown from five answers; the employer name stays with the member.

METRICS.label: Used at work
METRICS.definition: Members who reported using a course at work, over members who answered with the outcome grant on.
METRICS.note: Self-reported by the member; an employer report needs a data agreement.

METRICS.label: Platform return
METRICS.definition: Cost per verified competency, and employer ramp saved, as the parties report them.
METRICS.note: Needs cost and employer data nobody has handed in.

METRICS.label: Time to competency
METRICS.definition: Days from the first verification of a skill to its tenth verified use.
METRICS.note: R132: the professional threshold is ten verified uses across courses.

METRICS.label: Task time against benchmark
METRICS.definition: Minutes to resolve a task against a published service-level baseline.
METRICS.note: R132: no baseline is published yet.

METRICS.label: Learning velocity
METRICS.definition: Verified steps in the twenty-eight days before the page clock, over verified steps in the twenty-eight days before those.
METRICS.note: R132: the page passes the clock; the projection reads none.

METRICS.label: Values recalled
METRICS.definition: Recall activities answered correctly, over recall activities answered, at the checkpoints reached.
METRICS.note: R140: the activity asks for a value the team recorded; the distractors come from the record.

METRICS.label: Scenarios applied
METRICS.definition: Applied scenarios answered correctly, over applied scenarios offered at the checkpoints reached.
METRICS.note: R140: an address inside the prefix, a free port on the host, the committed size doubled.

METRICS.label: Conflicts resolved
METRICS.definition: Conflicts the record found that are no longer present, over conflicts found, once the apply checkpoint is reached.
METRICS.note: R140: read from the record itself; the answer only says the team looked.

METRICS.label: Minutes on task
METRICS.definition: Whole minutes the member had tasks open on a visible tab, pauses and hidden tabs excluded; a count.
METRICS.note: R140: the timer the member can pause; measured, never rewarded.

PRACTICES.label: Least privilege
PRACTICES.definition: Every account, role and agent holds only the rights its task needs, and nothing it might need later.

PRACTICES.label: Retest to closure
PRACTICES.definition: A finding is closed only by a retest that shows the fix, and every finding ends Closed, Open or Risk accepted.

PRACTICES.label: Likelihood-times-impact scoring
PRACTICES.definition: Each risk is scored on a stated scale for likelihood and impact, and the score decides the order.

PRACTICES.label: Configuration record
PRACTICES.definition: Every device configuration is saved, versioned and compared after a change.

PRACTICES.label: Build record
PRACTICES.definition: A build is recorded step by step with firmware, versions and settings as it is made.

PRACTICES.label: Right-sizing
PRACTICES.definition: Resources are sized from measured use, reviewed and shrunk when the measurement says so.

PRACTICES.label: Architecture decision records
PRACTICES.definition: Each significant design choice is recorded with its context, options and consequences.

PRACTICES.label: Test and acceptance
PRACTICES.definition: A build is accepted against written tests with recorded results, not against a feeling that it works.

PRACTICES.label: Evidence by design
PRACTICES.definition: Every control names the evidence that proves it operates, and the evidence is collected as the work happens.

PRACTICES.label: Redact before write
PRACTICES.definition: Personal data is detected and removed before a prompt, a log or a dataset is stored.

PRACTICES.label: Human checkpoint
PRACTICES.definition: AI-assisted work passes a named human check before it is acted on, and the check is recorded.

PRACTICES.label: Suites with a pass line
PRACTICES.definition: An attack or evaluation suite states what passing means before it runs.

SCORING.label: Tool proficiency
SCORING.definition: Commands and skills proven by output, and skills proved on a second task, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Reads browser checks and receipts of stamps, not proof of the machine; the per-tool table names each command.

SCORING.label: Troubleshooting success
SCORING.definition: Faults resolved, retries that verified, stuck flags cleared and steps resolved within the hour, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Faults are team rows; the minutes are a median between two recorded stamps, so a step left open overnight is counted apart.

SCORING.label: Judgment
SCORING.definition: Decisions recorded, justified and approved, and changes with a rollback written, equally weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Counts what was written against named options; it does not judge whether the choice was right.

SCORING.label: Collaboration
SCORING.definition: Hand-offs closed, RACI respected and peer reviews given, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Team facts count for the team; the role share on the KPIs says what this member moved.

SCORING.label: Reliability
SCORING.definition: On time against the cohort calendar, document control complete, controls cited and instructor approval, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: On time needs the cohort start date; without one the score stands on the other three and says so.

SCORING.label: Readiness
SCORING.definition: Exam weight verified, work-role coverage, skills retained and steps in order, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: A reading of the record against an exam and a work role, not a prediction of a pass or a hire.

SCORING.label: Understanding retained
SCORING.definition: Values recalled, scenarios applied and conflicts resolved, weeks after the team recorded them, weighted.
SCORING.caveat: Asks only about values the team recorded; before the checkpoint week the score stands on nothing and says so.

STANDARDS.label: NIST CSF
STANDARDS.description: NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
STANDARDS.why: Organises all security work into six functions. Tagging a step here shows which part of the lifecycle it strengthens and proves the work covered the whole picture, not just attack or defence.

STANDARDS.label: CIS
STANDARDS.description: CIS Critical Security Controls v8 and the CIS Benchmarks
STANDARDS.why: A prioritised "do these first" list of safeguards. A CIS tag means this step implements an industry-baseline control that auditors and blue teams recognise at once.

STANDARDS.label: NIST 800-61
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-61 Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
STANDARDS.why: The incident-handling playbook: prepare, detect and analyse, contain, eradicate, recover, learn. This tag means the step is part of a defensible, court-ready incident response process.

STANDARDS.label: NIST 800-115
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-115 Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
STANDARDS.why: The standard method for security testing and assessment. Following it makes scanning and exploitation repeatable, authorised and credible in a report.

STANDARDS.label: ISO 27001
STANDARDS.why: The certifiable information security management standard. This tag means the step produces the documented policy or evidence an ISO 27001 audit expects to see.

STANDARDS.label: SOC 2
STANDARDS.description: AICPA Trust Services Criteria for a SOC 2 examination
STANDARDS.why: The AICPA attestation standard built on the Trust Services Criteria: Security is CC1 to CC9, plus Availability, Confidentiality and the rest. This tag means the step produces a control or the evidence a SOC 2 Type I or II examiner samples.

STANDARDS.label: ITIL 4
STANDARDS.description: ITIL 4 service management practices: change, incident, problem, release
STANDARDS.why: The operating disciplines a network team is judged on: change, incident and problem management. A tag here means the step is not just technically right but done the way an organisation can audit: requested, reviewed, reversible and recorded.

STANDARDS.label: Well-Architected
STANDARDS.description: Well-Architected Framework pillars, Azure and AWS
STANDARDS.why: Both clouds judge a design on the same pillars: reliability, security, cost, operational excellence and performance. A tag here means the step is a design choice one of them would ask about.

STANDARDS.label: NIST AI RMF
STANDARDS.description: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 and its Generative AI Profile
STANDARDS.why: The AI framework Ridgeline adopts: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. A tag here means the step produces something an AI risk register or the AI questions a buyer asks will ask for.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-53
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 security and privacy controls
STANDARDS.why: The federal control catalogue the sixteen CISSP control statements are drawn from (PM-1, SC-7, AC-2). A tag here means the step writes or proves one of those controls.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-30
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-30 Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments
STANDARDS.why: The federal method for a risk assessment: threat sources, events, likelihood and impact. A risk register that follows it can be defended line by line.

STANDARDS.label: NIST SP 800-218
STANDARDS.description: NIST SP 800-218 Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)
STANDARDS.why: The practices a secure software pipeline follows: protect the code, produce well-secured software, respond to vulnerabilities. A pipeline record that cites it names the gate each practice became.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC 27005
STANDARDS.why: The risk method behind ISO 27001 clause 6: identify, analyse, evaluate, treat. A risk register that cites it reads the same way to an auditor.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC 27037
STANDARDS.description: ISO/IEC 27037 identification, collection, acquisition and preservation of digital evidence
STANDARDS.why: How evidence is collected and kept so it still counts later: identify, collect, acquire, preserve, with a chain of custody. An evidence log that cites it can be trusted in a dispute.

STANDARDS.label: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010
STANDARDS.why: What an architecture description must contain: stakeholders, concerns, viewpoints and the decisions behind them. A solution architecture document that cites it is complete rather than a diagram.

CUSTODY_RULES: Preserve the original — work on copies; never edit or rename the original artifact after collection.
Name every artifact `YYYYMMDD_TeamXX_Tool_Action.ext` so it is dated, attributed and self-describing.
Hash on collection: `sha256sum <file> >> Evidence_Hashes.txt`. Verify on receipt/before reporting: `sha256sum -c Evidence_Hashes.txt`.
Log every artifact in this file the moment it is collected — and log every hand-off (who → who, when).
Keep every artifact for a week in `~/team-artifacts/week-N/`; the team package gathers them into `04_Testing_and_Findings/Evidence/`. Keep originals read-only and backed up.
One custodian holds the evidence at a time; record each transfer so the chain is unbroken.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The terminal doesn’t recognise the program — usually a typo or the tool isn’t installed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the spelling. If it’s really missing, install it: sudo apt update && sudo apt install <tool>

variants.otherwise: — the step that first uses a tool says how to install it.

ERROR_ROWS.fix: Add sudo in front on Linux (sudo <command>). On Windows/PowerShell, close it and reopen with “Run as administrator”.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Connection refused / No route to host / host seems down
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You can’t reach the target — it’s off, the IP is wrong, or you’re not on the right network.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: ping the address first. Confirm the machine is powered on and that you are on the same subnet as it

variants.then: , and that you set the right IP in Lab access.
variants.otherwise: — a host in another zone only answers once the route between them exists.

variants.then: For nmap, add -Pn to scan a host that blocks ping.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You’re in the wrong folder, or the path/filename is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run pwd to see where you are and cd ~ to go home.

variants.then: For hydra, rockyou is gzipped by default — unzip it once: sudo gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz
variants.otherwise: Check the file really exists with ls before you edit it — a config path is easy to mistype.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: That’s a placeholder, not a real address — you copied it literally.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Open the Lab access panel at the top of the Tasks tab and enter {label}; the site then fills it into every command automatically.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: ssh: connect to host … Operation timed out (from home)
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Your laptop is not on the tailnet, or the host is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the Tailscale client is signed in and connected on your laptop, then run tailscale status on the host — it must list the host as online. On campus you can still reach it on its 10.10.30.T address while you sort this out.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: The Proxmox console times out but SSH works
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The path is fine; the web service or the port is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run systemctl status pveproxy --no-pager over SSH. Remember the console is on port 8006 and https, not http — a plain http:// URL simply hangs.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: It worked yesterday and not today
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The host rebooted and something did not come back, or your address changed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: systemctl is-active tailscaled on the host must read active. The host keeps the same Tailscale address across reboots, so if the address you saved has changed, you are looking at a rebuilt host that was re-authorised as a new device.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Permission denied (publickey) after setting up keys
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The key is not where the server expects it, or the account is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run ssh -v to see which key is offered, and confirm you are connecting as the right user. Password login is still enabled until Week 4 hardens it, so you have a way back in — use it rather than locking yourself out further.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The VM cannot reach the Core over the ops network — the second NIC, the VLAN tag or the bridge is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: On the host, ip -br a must show vmbr9 UP with the team’s 10.20.T.1 address. Inside the VM, the second interface needs its 10.20.T.x address and no gateway. Still nothing: the switch port is not trunking VLAN 20 — the Networking deep-dive owns that.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Some commands (a bare ping, a large download, a package install) run until you stop them, or they’re waiting on a slow or unreachable host.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Press Ctrl+C to stop it. Re-check reachability (ping), and give a genuinely long job a minute

variants.otherwise: — an OS install or a big apt upgrade takes minutes, not seconds.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: When anything fails, the error’s last line usually names the real problem.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Match that line to the rows above. Also double-check you’re on the machine the step’s WHERE chip names — running the right command on the wrong host is the most common cause.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Open a terminal
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: On a Linux desktop, click the black terminal icon or press Ctrl+Alt+T. On a server you reach over SSH, the terminal is the session itself. You type commands here and press Enter to run them.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: The prompt
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: A line ending in $ (or #) is the prompt — it means the terminal is waiting for you. You don’t type the $ itself.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Paste a command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Copy from this site, then in the terminal press Ctrl+Shift+V (plain Ctrl+V often does nothing in a terminal). Right-click → Paste also works.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Run one line at a time
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: When a step shows several numbered commands, run them one by one — paste one, press Enter, wait for it to finish, then the next.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: sudo = run as admin
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: sudo runs a command with admin rights (it may ask for your password — typing shows nothing, that’s normal). On Windows/PowerShell, instead right-click PowerShell → “Run as administrator”.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Stop a stuck command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Press Ctrl+C to cancel a command that hangs or runs forever (e.g. a ping with no -c limit).
